197.title: Contentment is wealth (201–204)
197.hook: victory breeds hatred; health is the greatest gift, contentment the greatest wealth (Dhammapada 204)
197.howItsDone: Contentment with little is one of the qualities Buddhist monastics are trained in, and lay Buddhists often quote verse 204 as everyday wisdom about health, enough and trust.

segments.voice: Yesterday, sukha: happy among the hating, fed by joy with an empty bowl. Your line was we live happily.

You get the raise. For about two weeks it feels wonderful. Then the new number becomes the normal number, and you start noticing what the next one would buy. Or you win the argument, the other person goes quiet, and somehow the room feels worse than before. It's a finish line that keeps moving. There's a word for being able to stop at the line you're already standing on, and today's verse calls it the best kind of money there is.

segments.voice: Verse two oh one, in Max Müller's words: "Victory breeds hatred, for the conquered is unhappy. He who has given up both victory and defeat, he, the contented, is happy." The commentary says the Buddha spoke it after King Pasenadi of Kosala lost a battle to his own nephew and couldn't eat or sleep for shame. Winning makes an enemy; losing makes you miserable. The only way out of that seesaw is to step off it. Then the chapter's great list, verse two oh four: "Health is the greatest of gifts, contentedness the best riches; trust is the best of relationships, Nirvana the highest happiness." The Pali for contentment is santuṭṭhi, being satisfied with what's there. It isn't laziness, or giving up on improving things. It's the ability to stop feeling poor when you have enough. There's a lovely story behind that verse too. The same King Pasenadi, the commentary says, ate so much at every meal that he could barely stay awake to hear the Buddha teach. The Buddha suggested he eat a little less, mindfully. The king had his nephew recite a short verse at every meal as a reminder, cut back bit by bit, grew slim and well, and came back to thank him. Health, the greatest gift. And notice where the list ends: trust as the best kinship, and nibbāna, the deepest ease, as the highest happiness. None of the four is for sale.

198.title: Good company (205–208)
198.hook: to see the noble is good; follow the wise as the moon follows the path of the stars
198.howItsDone: Buddhists place great weight on kalyāṇamitta, good spiritual friendship, through teachers, the monastic community and fellow practitioners, and many see visiting a respected monk or nun as a blessing in itself.

segments.voice: Yesterday, santuṭṭhi: health the greatest gift, enough the best riches. Your line was health is the greatest gift.

Think of someone you always feel a little better after seeing. Not because they flatter you. Maybe they're just steady. They listen all the way to the end of your sentence. They don't gossip, and around them you don't either. You leave the coffee standing a bit straighter. Now think of someone who has the opposite effect. You know exactly who. We become, slowly, like the people we spend our hours with. Chapter fifteen ends with that simple and slightly uncomfortable truth.

segments.voice: Verse two oh six, in Max Müller's translation: "The sight of the elect (Arya) is good, to live with them is always happiness". Ariya means noble, not by birth but by character: someone well along the path. Just seeing such a person, the verse says, is good. Then verse two oh seven: "company with the wise is pleasure, like meeting with kinsfolk." Like coming home to family. And the closing image, verse two oh eight: "one ought to follow a good and wise man, as the moon follows the path of the stars." In old India, the moon's path through the sky was traced along a ring of star groups, the lunar mansions. The moon doesn't wander at random; it keeps to a known road. Good friends are that road. The Buddha put this more strongly than you might expect. In one discourse, his attendant Ānanda says that good friendship must be half of the holy life. The Buddha corrects him: not half. It's the whole of the holy life. The Pali phrase is kalyāṇamitta, a lovely friend, a good friend, someone whose company leans you toward the good. The verses also say that time with fools is painful, and that's worth reading carefully. Buddhists don't take it as permission to look down on anyone. It's about whose habits you're soaking in, day after day, and choosing on purpose. You will soak something in. The only question is what.

199.title: From the dear, grief (209–216)
199.hook: from what is dear comes grief, from what is dear comes fear; one free of it has neither
199.howItsDone: Buddhist monastics leave close family ties behind, and some teachers present these verses to lay people as a call to love without clinging, and to meet loss with the understanding that everything dear will change.

segments.voice: Yesterday, good company: follow the wise, as the moon follows the stars. Your line was keep good company. Today, chapter sixteen begins.

A stranger's phone falls in a lake, and nobody loses sleep. A coworker's cousin has surgery, and the day goes on. But a parent's kid is ten minutes late, and the stomach starts to knot. A dog limps, and the whole evening goes gray. The things we love are exactly the things that can hurt us, and still, people go on loving. Chapter sixteen of the Dhammapada looks at that trade with unusual honesty.
screen: `A STRANGER'S PHONE IN THE LAKE.` → `A KID, TEN MINUTES LATE.` → `WHAT WE LOVE CAN HURT US.`

segments.voice: Chapter sixteen is called Piyavagga. Piya means dear, beloved, precious; Müller titled it pleasure, but dear is closer. Verse two twelve, in his words: "From pleasure comes grief, from pleasure comes fear; he who is free from pleasure knows neither grief nor fear." In Pali: from what is dear comes sorrow, from what is dear comes fear. The next four verses repeat it with other words: from affection, from lust, from love, from craving. Five times, the same shape. There's a story in the Udāna, one of the early collections. Visākhā, a devoted lay follower of the Buddha, came to him in wet clothes and wet hair, grieving a grandchild who had died. He asked her: would you like as many children and grandchildren as there are people in this city? Yes, she said. And how many people die in this city each day? Many, she said. Then, he answered gently, you'd never be without wet clothes and wet hair. Those who have a hundred dear ones have a hundred sorrows. Those who have none have none. This is hard teaching, and verse two eleven goes further, in Müller's words: "Let, therefore, no man love anything; loss of the beloved is evil." Buddhists read that in more than one way. Some take it strictly, as monastics do when they leave close family ties behind. Some teachers read it as being about grasping: love fully, hold loosely, knowing that everything dear will change. The tradition's own loving-kindness, metta, wishes all beings well without clutching any of them. Either way, the verses tell the truth about love's cost.

200.title: Welcomed home (217–220)
200.hook: as kin welcome a traveler home, good deeds welcome the one who did good
200.howItsDone: Many Buddhists make merit through giving, keeping precepts and practice, and often dedicate that merit to others; these verses are commonly cited to describe good deeds as what goes with a person beyond this life.

segments.voice: Yesterday, piya: from what is dear comes grief, and Visākhā in wet clothes. Your line was love fully, hold loosely.

At the arrivals gate of an airport, the doors slide open, and someone walks out after a long time away: a soldier, a student back from a year abroad, a grandmother who flew halfway around the world. A little crowd is waiting. Balloons, a handmade sign, a kid who breaks loose and runs. Nobody at that gate is thinking about the traveler's résumé. They're just glad. Today's verse takes that gate and puts it somewhere unexpected.

segments.voice: Chapter sixteen spends its first verses on the grief that comes from what is dear. It ends with what is dear in a good way. Verse two seventeen, in Max Müller's words, describes a person the world holds dear: one with virtue and insight, who is just, speaks the truth, and "does what is his own business". Then the two verses today is named for. Verse two nineteen: "Kinsmen, friends, and lovers salute a man who has been long away, and returns safe from afar." And verse two twenty: "In like manner his good works receive him who has done good, and has gone from this world to the other;--as kinsmen receive a friend on his return." The Pali word for those good works is puñña, often translated merit: goodness that builds up, like savings. In Buddhist teaching, a person continues after death according to their actions, and here the actions themselves are pictured as family at the gate. The old commentary gives it a story. A generous man named Nandiya built a hall for the monks. The great disciple Moggallāna, the story says, visited a heaven realm and saw a mansion already being prepared there for Nandiya, before Nandiya had even died. Even without picturing heaven, the image is easy to hold: in this verse, a kind deed is sent on ahead, and when the doer arrives, it's waiting at the gate like family with a handmade sign.

201.title: Hold the chariot (221–222)
201.hook: one who holds back rising anger like a rolling chariot is a real driver; others only hold the reins
201.carry: other people are but holding the reins
201.howItsDone: Buddhists practice restraining anger as it arises, by noticing it in the body, pausing and breathing, and many recite the Buddha's title 'the incomparable trainer of those who can be tamed' in daily chanting.

segments.voice: Yesterday, welcomed home: good deeds waiting at the gate like family. Your line was good deeds greet you. Today, chapter seventeen begins: anger.

Anyone can hold a steering wheel. On an empty road on a sunny day, everyone's a fine driver. The real test comes when a car cuts you off, or the road turns to ice, or the kid in the back seat spills the juice right as the light turns yellow. That's when you find out whether you're driving or just holding on. Anger works the same way: everyone is patient when nothing is pushing. Chapter seventeen of the Dhammapada is about anger, and its second verse hands out a job title worth having.
screen: `ANYONE CAN HOLD A WHEEL.` → `ICE, A CUT-OFF, SPILLED JUICE.` → `DRIVING, OR JUST HOLDING ON?`

segments.voice: The chapter opens with verse two twenty-one, in Max Müller's translation: "Let a man leave anger, let him forsake pride, let him overcome all bondage!" Then the image, verse two twenty-two: "He who holds back rising anger like a rolling chariot, him I call a real driver; other people are but holding the reins." Picture a chariot in the ancient world: horses at full gallop, wooden wheels, no brakes. Once it's rolling, stopping it takes real strength and skill. Anger, the verse says, is like that. It arises, gathers speed, and wants to run. Holding it back isn't the same as never feeling it. The skill is in not letting it run over anyone. The Pali word for anger is kodha, and the verse's word for the real driver is sārathi, a charioteer: the same word Buddhists use in one of the Buddha's titles, the incomparable trainer of those who can be tamed. The old commentary gives the verse a surprising story. A monk, clearing ground for a hut, cut down a tree and injured the child of the spirit who lived in it. The tree spirit, furious, raised her hand to strike him. And then she stopped. She held it back. She went to the Buddha and told him, and he praised her with this very verse. A real driver isn't the one who never feels the horses pull. It's the one who feels them pull, hard, and still holds the chariot.

Now, in your mind, take the reins, not by fighting the horses but by leaning back, slowing, one breath at a time, until you're the one driving.

202.title: Overcome anger by kindness (223–228)
202.hook: overcome anger by not-anger, evil by good, the miser by giving, the liar by truth; no one is never blamed
202.howItsDone: Teachers often turn to verse 223 when they speak about patience, and many Buddhists practice meeting hostility with calm and generosity, often supported by loving-kindness meditation toward difficult people.

segments.voice: Yesterday, kodha: a real driver holds back rising anger; the rest only hold the reins. Your line was other people are but holding the reins.
screen: `OTHER PEOPLE ARE BUT HOLDING THE REINS.`

segments.voice: Someone is rude to you at the checkout. The obvious move is to match them: a little coldness back, a sigh, maybe a comment. It feels fair. And then you both walk away a bit worse than you arrived. Now picture the other move. You say, it's been a long day for you, hasn't it, and smile. Sometimes the other person softens right there. Sometimes they don't. But something in you stays clean either way. Yesterday was about stopping the chariot; today's verse is about which direction to drive it.
screen: `RUDE AT THE CHECKOUT.` → `MATCH THEM, OR THE OTHER MOVE.` → `WHICH DIRECTION TO DRIVE.`

segments.voice: Verse two twenty-three, in Max Müller's translation: "Let a man overcome anger by love, let him overcome evil by good; let him overcome the greedy by liberality, the liar by truth!" Four pairs, each fought with the opposite weapon. Müller wrote love, but the Pali is akkodha, simply non-anger, calm. You don't beat anger by being angrier; you beat it by not joining in. Harm is met with good, stinginess with generosity, lies with truth. It only works if you refuse the other person's weapon. Then the chapter turns to something that makes this easier: you'll be criticized no matter what. The commentary tells of a layman named Atula who went with friends to hear a teaching. The first monk they visited sat in silence, and Atula grumbled that he said nothing. The next, Sāriputta, gave a long, deep teaching, and Atula grumbled that it was too long. The next, Ānanda, spoke briefly: too short. Finally he went to the Buddha, who told him, in verse two twenty-seven, that this was an old saying: they blame the silent, they blame the talkative, they blame the one who says little, "there is no one on earth who is not blamed." And verse two twenty-eight: "There never was, there never will be, nor is there now, a man who is always blamed, or a man who is always praised." If blame is guaranteed, you're free. You might as well answer with kindness.

203.title: Three doors guarded (229–234)
203.hook: guard against anger of the body, of the tongue, of the mind
203.carry: the mind is where anger first knocks
203.howItsDone: Buddhist ethics sorts action into three doors, body, speech and mind, and the ten wholesome courses of action (three of body, four of speech, three of mind) are a common framework for daily reflection and confession.

segments.voice: Yesterday, akkodha: four harms, four opposite weapons, and Atula, who blamed everyone. Your line was overcome by giving. Today ends the week.

A house has three doors: a front door, a back door, and a side door by the garage. You can lock the front door every night, but if the side door is wide open, anyone can walk in. Anger is like a visitor who tries every door. Some of us guard our hands well: we'd never hit anyone. But the tongue is wide open. Or we're careful with words, and the mind is running a whole courtroom drama in the background. Chapter seventeen ends by checking every door in the house.

segments.voice: First, a picture of a person nobody could honestly blame: like a coin of gold from the Jambu river, praised even by the gods. The way there: guard three doors. Verse two thirty-one, in Max Müller's translation: "Beware of bodily anger, and control thy body!" Verse two thirty-two: "Beware of the anger of the tongue, and control thy tongue!" And verse two thirty-three: "Beware of the anger of the mind, and control thy mind!" Each verse has two halves: stop the harm through that door, and use that same door for good. The body that could strike can also help. The tongue that could wound can also comfort. Then the chapter's last line, verse two thirty-four: "The wise who control their body, who control their tongue, the wise who control their mind, are indeed well controlled." Buddhist teaching calls these the three doors of action: body, speech and mind, in Pali kāya, vacī and mano. Every action, it says, goes out through one of them. That's why the ten classic wholesome actions are sorted this way: three for the body, four for speech, three for the mind. Notice which comes last. The mind is where anger first knocks, long before the tongue or the hand. Now look back at the week, a house with good doors. Health is the greatest gift. Keep good company. Love fully, hold loosely. Good deeds greet you. Other people are but holding the reins. Overcome by giving. And today: three doors guarded.

segments.voice: Check each door in turn, the body first: notice your hands, your shoulders, your jaw, and let anything clenched soften. Then the tongue: if a sharp sentence is waiting behind your teeth, let it rest there, unspoken. Then the mind: if an argument is running in the background, notice it, and let it quiet down on the out-breath, three doors closed to anger and open to kindness.
Dvāra. A door, a gate: verses two thirty-one to two thirty-four say guard against anger of the body, of the tongue and of the mind, and use each for good.
Your line: the mind is where anger first knocks. Body, tongue, mind: one house, well kept. That closes the week.
